analysis.one_liner: Bans unlicensed emergency shelters holding migrant children, including Tornillo, Texas and Homestead, Florida.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate's final two weeks with no cosponsors, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Department of Health and Human Services from running or contracting any unlicensed 'temporary emergency shelter' for unaccompanied migrant children, and would explicitly close the large shelters then operating in Tornillo, Texas and Homestead, Florida. Children in federal custody would instead have to be placed in facilities that meet state child-welfare licensing standards. The bill was introduced on December 19, 2018, with the 115th Congress set to end two weeks later, and died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Unaccompanied migrant children in federal custody, who would be moved out of large, unlicensed tent-style shelters and into facilities licensed under state child-welfare standards. Federal court monitors and child-welfare advocates had raised concerns about conditions and length of stay at these shelters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unaccompanied migrant children in federal custody

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits HHS from operating or contracting any unlicensed temporary emergency shelter for unaccompanied migrant children, requiring care in licensed facilities instead [S3].
Explicitly names and would shut down the shelters at Tornillo, Texas and Homestead, Florida, the two large unlicensed camps then operating [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would likely bear somewhat higher per-child costs, since licensed facilities with state child-welfare standards generally cost more than tent shelters. Private contractors operating the unlicensed shelters would lose their federal contracts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shelter contractors and federal detention budgets

drawbacks.text: Licensed capacity for unaccompanied children was limited; the CRS summary notes these shelters existed because licensed facilities were 'near or at capacity,' so an immediate shutdown could have forced faster releases or transfers without enough licensed beds [S2].
The bill was introduced with no cosponsors in the final two weeks of the Congress and contained no transition plan for the children already held at the named shelters [S4] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — requiring every facility holding migrant children to meet state child-care licensing standards — addresses a real gap, since unlicensed shelters operate outside the state inspections that licensed facilities face. The main cost is logistical: licensed capacity is limited, so a ban would require rapid movement of children into licensed beds or release to sponsors. The bill offered no transition mechanism, but that flaw is small relative to the licensing guarantee it would create.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with two weeks left in the Congress and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never took it up before the session ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the bill on December 19, 2018 [S1] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, so the bill died in committee without a hearing or vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The operators of the unlicensed shelters kept their federal contracts; the children at Tornillo and Homestead stayed in unlicensed care. Tornillo closed days later as its own contract wound down, but Homestead continued operating into the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shelter contractors, not the detained children

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its unlicensed-shelter ban; recruited no cosponsors before the session ended.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held no hearing or markup on the bill in the two weeks remaining before Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the Senate floor calendar in the final two weeks of the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor, and no colleague joined as a cosponsor during the session's final days.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only party-line facts: a lone Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, referred to a Republican-run committee that took no action in the session's final two weeks.

industries.industry: Private shelter contractors for unaccompanied migrant children
industries.note: The bill would end HHS contracts with unlicensed facilities like Tornillo and Homestead, which were run by private operators. Those firms' revenue came from holding children in facilities exempt from state child-welfare licensing, so their interest in the bill ran directly against the children's.
Requiring care in licensed facilities would shift funding toward regulated providers that meet state child-care standards, which serves the same goal as protecting the children in custody.
